hook: You know the saying that God never gives you more than you can handle. But did you know 1 Corinthians 10:13 is about temptation?
story:
Paul reaches for one of the darkest moments in his people’s memory. They had walked out of Egypt with the waters standing like a wall on either side. They were camped at the mountain where God had met them. And with Moses gone up the mountain, they made a calf of gold, held a feast and “sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play”.

Paul quotes that very sentence to the Corinthians. Some of them felt strong enough to sit at table in an idol’s temple (1 Corinthians 8:10). His warning is gentle and unsparing at once: the people who fell in the wilderness were no strangers to God. They had passed through the sea.

Then, at the point of greatest danger, comes the kindness. No temptation is unique. God is faithful. And he does not leave anyone without a door: “the way of escape”.
moment:
The young church in Corinth was full of confidence. Some of its members were sure their faith was strong enough for anything. They could sit down to eat in an idol’s temple, they thought, and it would not touch them.

Paul loves these people and he is worried for them. He does not call them weak. He tells them a story about people who were just as sure, and he ends it with a sentence aimed straight at their confidence: “let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn’t fall”. Only then does he give them the promise.
around: The verse speaks of temptation: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape”. The next verse says what to do with that: “flee from idolatry”.
after:
The warning did not settle everything in Corinth. Paul’s next letter shows how painful the time that followed was. He had made up his mind not to come to them “again in sorrow”, and he had written to them “with many tears”, not to hurt them, he says, but so that they would know how much he loved them.

Then Titus came back from Corinth. Paul had reached Macedonia with no rest: “Fightings were outside. Fear was inside.” Now he heard of their longing, their mourning and their zeal for him. They had been “grieved to repentance”, and Paul, who had regretted sending that hard letter, writes that he rejoiced.

The church needed calling back again. Later in the first century, most likely in the 90s, a few headstrong, self-confident people turned the church in Corinth against its elders and removed some of them. The church in Rome wrote to them, in a letter early Christian writers credit to Clement. It told the Corinthians to take up Paul’s old letter once more, the one he had written when the gospel was new among them, and it urged them to fall down before the Lord and ask, with tears, to be reconciled.

Around the year 170, Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, mentioned in a letter to Rome that his church read Clement’s letter in its gatherings, and the historian Eusebius took this to show that it had been their custom from the beginning. A church that had to be called back more than once kept the letters that called it back, and went on reading them aloud.
readings:
In everyday speech this verse has become a saying about suffering: God will not give you more than you can handle. People say it to comfort one another at hospital beds and funerals, and they mean it kindly.

The verse itself is about temptation. It promises that no pull toward wrong is too strong to resist, because God always leaves a way out.

Many pastors gently point out the difference, because the saying can hurt. Some burdens are more than a person can carry, and Paul knew it. He wrote that he had been “weighed down exceedingly, beyond our power”. The comfort of the Bible in such times is not that the load will be light. It is that no one is asked to carry it alone.
argued:
Around the year 400 Augustine looked honestly at himself in his Confessions. He did not know, he admitted, which temptations he could resist and which he could not. His hope rested on this verse: [[augustine-temptation]]

A thousand years later Thomas à Kempis wrote in The Imitation of Christ that temptation does not come to everyone in the same measure: [[kempis]] For him that was no reason to despair. It was a reason to cry out to God all the more.

In our own time the verse has turned into a saying: God will not give you more than you can handle. One version even travels under Mother Teresa’s name, but the Mother Teresa Center lists it among the quotes falsely attributed to her. The pastor John Piper has answered the saying directly. The limit Paul speaks of, he says, is [[piper]]

From a bishop who did not trust his own strength to a pastor correcting a well-meant saying, the comfort rests in the same place: God is faithful.
point: The promise is about temptation to sin, and it comes with a way out and a command to take it. It does not say that suffering will never be more than a person can bear. Paul himself writes elsewhere that he and his companions “were weighed down exceedingly, beyond our power” (2 Corinthians 1:8).
lesson:
It is easy to believe that your struggle is unusual, that nobody else would understand it. This verse says the opposite: “No temptation has taken you except what is common to man.” Whatever pulls at you, you are not the first.

Notice where Paul puts the weight. Not on how strong you are, but on this: “God is faithful”. And he speaks of a door, “the way of escape”. That door often looks very ordinary: leaving the room, closing the screen, telling a friend, saying no before the moment comes close. The door is there, but you still have to walk through it. Paul’s very next words to the Corinthians were to flee.

If you are sure you are past all this, read verse 12 again, slowly. And if you have already fallen, remember that Paul later rejoiced over these same people because they grieved and turned back. You can bring it to God honestly, today, and ask him for help with the next step.

If you do not share this faith, the verse still names something true about people: we are rarely in more danger than when we are sure we are safe.

echoes.note: The one we turn to is no stranger to temptation. He was “in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.” So the letter invites us to come to him for “help in time of need.”
On the night Peter was sure he would never fall, Jesus told him, “Watch and pray, that you don’t enter into temptation.” The way out often starts before the moment comes.
Joseph did not argue with the temptation. He “left his garment in her hand, and ran outside.” It cost him his coat, and soon his freedom, but it was a way out, and he took it.
